title: Australia's Fair Work Commission will require AI-use disclosure from October 20
subtitle: The rule follows a surge in unrepresented litigants filing AI-assisted cases — 40% of surveyed applicants used generative AI, and the Commission is now condemning 'plain wrong' AI legal advice.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Australia's Fair Work Commission — the country's federal workplace-relations tribunal — will require applicants and their representatives to disclose whether they used generative AI to prepare a case, and how, starting October 20, 2026. The rule follows internal surveys finding that roughly 40 percent of recent applicants had used generative AI to draft submissions or manage their case, with about 77 percent of those using ChatGPT. The Commission cited a rising volume of submissions containing what it called 'plain wrong' AI-generated legal claims and fabricated citations — the same hallucinated-caselaw problem that has drawn sanctions from courts in the U.S., Canada and the U.K. since 2023.

The disclosure regime is the softer of the two approaches available: rather than banning AI-assisted filings, the Commission is requiring transparency and warning that misuse can affect cost orders. That is a considered response to a real access-to-justice tension. In the same week the Commission adopted the rule, a Macquarie University academic named Gregory Baker won a landmark unfair-treatment case representing himself against the university with the help of paid ChatGPT and Claude tiers — the first successful test of Labor's 2024 'employee choice pathway' reforms, and a case that likely would not have been brought without AI-assisted preparation.

That tension — AI is enabling people who could not previously afford representation to bring real cases, and it is simultaneously flooding the tribunal with confidently-wrong submissions — is now the operative policy question for every tribunal-level body worldwide. Australia's answer, disclosure plus a cost-order stick, is one point on the spectrum. The U.S. federal courts have gone farther in some districts, requiring counsel to certify that AI-generated text was verified against real cases. The E.U. and U.K. have mostly stayed with judge-by-judge practice directions. Australia's choice will be watched.

For learners: if you ever draft anything meant for a court, a tribunal, an agency, or a regulator, every citation an AI produces has to be independently verified before it goes in the filing. Not spot-checked — every one. Hallucinated caselaw looks exactly like real caselaw until you open the actual reporter, and the failure mode is not embarrassment, it is sanction. That verification step is now table stakes for using AI in any adversarial process.
